title: Journeys east and a new town
hookLine: Guru Tegh Bahadur travels as far as Assam and founds the town that becomes Anandpur

lines: A NEW HOME, AND THE ROAD.
cards: Two suitcases and a rented shop in a new country. A cheap old house, fixed up one room at a time after a hard year. Starting over takes a kind of courage that isn't loud at all.

Guru Tegh Bahadur, the new ninth Guru, did not have an easy welcome. Some of the disappointed claimants turned hostile; tradition says one of them even had a shot fired at him. So the quiet Guru did two things.
He built a new home, and he set out on a long road east.

teach.b: First, the town. In 1665 the Guru bought land in the Shivalik foothills, near Kiratpur, from the ruling family of the hill state of Kahlur. He named the settlement Chakk Nanaki, after his mother, Mata Nanaki.
It was rough ground by the river Sutlej, with hills behind.
Over the years it would grow into a Sikh center known as Anandpur, the city of bliss. You met the word anand on day fifty-three, in the song of bliss. Much of the rest of this camp happens there.
Second, the journey. Soon after founding the town, the Guru set out east, the way Guru Nanak had gone long before, visiting Sikh communities and holy places.
He traveled through Agra and Allahabad, to Benares, and on to Patna, on the Ganges.

There he left his wife, Mata Gujri, who was expecting a child, and kept going: to Dhaka, in Bengal, and all the way to Assam, in the far east, where tradition says he helped make peace between an imperial army and the Assamese kingdom.
While he was far away, his son was born in Patna. The Guru would not see him for years. The quiet man from the room below ground didn't wait for a perfect life.
He took rough land and started a town. He took the road and strengthened scattered communities.
Build where you are, with what you have, and let it grow into something you may never fully see.

how: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib, the town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur, and gurdwaras mark his travels in the east, from Patna and Dhaka to Dhubri in Assam.

o: the city of bliss, grown from a town on rough ground
the village where the twenty-two claimants gathered
the city in the east where the Guru's son was born

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the new town, named for his mother

s: the town was first called Anandpur
he named it Chakk Nanaki, after his mother; it grew into Anandpur.
the Guru traveled as far east as Assam
through Benares and Patna, to Dhaka, and on to Assam.
the Guru was at home in Patna when his son was born
he had traveled on east; he would not see his son for years.

games.q: you're the new Guru. some rivals are hostile, and one has even had a shot fired at you. what do you do?
o: fight them for control of Bakala.
found a new town, and take to the road.
games.why: he bought land and founded Chakk Nanaki, later Anandpur, then set out east to visit Sikh communities as far as Assam.

practice: Think of something you've wanted to begin but keep saving for when life is calmer: a habit, a project, a friendship, a garden. Picture the rough ground as it is now, not ideal, and the first small stake you could put in it.
If a seed, a pot or a notebook is near, you can even make that start now; if not, just hold the beginning.

wordCard.voice: Anandpur. The city of bliss that grew from Chakk Nanaki, the town Guru Tegh Bahadur founded near Kiratpur before journeying east as far as Assam.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; pur, town. The city of bliss.

carryVoice: Your line: build where you are. Rough ground was enough for a town. Day seventy-six.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on the founding of Chakk Nanaki (1665) and Guru Tegh Bahadur's eastern travels
